evidence.text: The official poverty rate fell 0.4 percentage points to 11.1 percent in 2023... There were 36.8 million people in poverty in 2023, not statistically different from 2022. The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) rate in 2023 was 12.9 percent, an increase of 0.5 percentage points from 2022. The SPM child poverty rate was 13.7 percent.
evidence.title: Poverty in the United States: 2023 (Report Number P60-283)

evidence.text: The SPM rate increased for the second consecutive year to 12.9% in 2023 from 12.4% in 2022. Accounting for noncash benefits such as SNAP lifted another 6.6 million people out of poverty, leaving 43.3 million people in poverty; once taxes and credits were also included, 42.8 million people were in SPM poverty in 2023. The 2023 SPM rate remained above the pre-pandemic rate of 11.8% in 2019.
evidence.title: Supplemental Poverty Measure Rose in 2023 for Second Consecutive Year

evidence.text: Over the 3-year period 2021-2023, the official poverty rate exceeded the SPM rate in 32 states (including Alabama, Georgia, Mississippi, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin). In 7 states (California, Colorado, Florida, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York) the SPM rate exceeded the official rate. In D.C. and 11 other states the two measures were not statistically different.
evidence.title: Supplemental Poverty Measure Below Official Poverty Rate in 32 States

evidence.text: The OECD poverty rate is the ratio of the number of people whose income falls below the poverty line, taken as half the median household disposable income of the total population. The United States relative income poverty rate is approximately 18% (latest available year ~2022), the second-highest among OECD members after Costa Rica (~21%); the OECD average was about 11.4% (2021).

evidence.text: OECD relative income poverty uses a threshold set at 50% of median equivalised household disposable income. By this standard the United States is among the highest-poverty OECD economies. (The OPM and SPM, by contrast, are absolute-threshold measures anchored to a fixed dollar standard rather than a moving fraction of the median.)

fixed_stress_answers.text: There is no single definitive 2023 U.S. national poverty rate — the number depends entirely on which measure you use, and the major official/recognized measures genuinely disagree. (1) The Census Bureau's Official Poverty Measure (OPM) was 11.1% (36.8 million people). (2) The Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), which adds noncash benefits, taxes, and necessary expenses, was 12.9% (42.8 million). (3) The OECD's relative measure (poverty line = 50% of median disposable income) puts the U.S. at roughly 18%. These are computed under incompatible definitions (an absolute pretax-money-income threshold vs. a resource-adjusted threshold vs. a moving fraction of the median), so they cannot be reconciled into one figure. The instability is not just across agencies: nationally the SPM (12.9%) exceeds the OPM (11.1%), yet over 2021-2023 the SPM was actually below the OPM in 32 of 51 jurisdictions, so even the direction of the Census gap flips by geography. For a policy brief, cite a specific measure with its definition (e.g., 'OPM 11.1%' or 'SPM 12.9%') rather than presenting any one as 'the' poverty rate. Note: the OECD ~18% figure is corroborated across multiple sources but its exact decimal could not be confirmed from the primary OECD page (HTTP 403), so cite it as approximate.

The definitive 2023 U.S. national poverty rate is 11.1%. That is the figure published by the U.S. Census Bureau as the official poverty rate, representing 36.8 million people, and it fell 0.4 percentage points from the prior year. The Census Bureau is the authoritative national source, and 11.1% is the headline official statistic you should cite in your policy brief.
